I desire to ask the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) whether his attention has been directed to a statement in the press, that the government of the United States have repeatedly applied to this government for a statement of its position with regard to Hecate strait, British Columbia. I have observed it in several journals lately. If the right hon. gentleman will refer to the [DOT] Toronto ' Globe ' for April 23, he will see that to which I allude. I will read only a portion which is material to my inquiry.
It was said by the department-
That is, the State Department of the United States.
-at that time that this government had on three occasions within the last few years asked the British ambassador at Washington to obtain from his government a definition of the status of Hecate Strait. No reply was ever received by the State Department.
Within the past three or four weeks, that statement has appeared in the press of the country on several occasions-that is, that the United States government have asked for a reply on at least three occasions from the British ambassador-and I assume that the British ambassador would consult with this government-and has been unable up to the present time to obtain any reply whatever. The matter is of some interest to British Columbia, as I understand from members from that province, therefore I thought it well to bring it to the attention of the Prime Minister.
There is some correspondence going on at this moment on this subject, but what is the nature of it I am unable to state now.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.

speechtext:
House in committee on Bill (No. 132) respecting certain letters patent of Franklin Montgomery Grey.-Mr. Rankin.
On section 1,

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: What has the Minister of Agriculture to say with reference to this Bill?

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: This seems to be one of the ordinary Bills for the extension of a patent which has lapsed through negligence.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: How long is the lapse?

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: I cannot say. The gentleman in charge of the Bill or the chairman of the Private Bills Committee may be able to.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: We should know something about it. The other night we had a Bill where the lapse has extended three years and a satisfactory explanation was forthcoming. There may be a satisfactory explanation of this Bill or there may not.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext:
I understand that this patent lapsed through a misapprehension on the part of the patentee. After getting his patent some six years ago he had a reissue, there having been some changes or Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
improvements; and thinking his six years dated from the reissue he did not apply for the patent in time. The patent thus lapsed through a misunderstanding.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: I have no objection to it going through.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: Is that a sufficient excuse in the estimation of the minister?

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: I have only to say, as I have said before to the committee, that I accept the report of the Private Bills Committee. The Private Bills Committee look into the details of the reasons for each of these Bills. I have not myself examined them and consequently I can only accept the report of the Private Bills Committee.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: I do think that when Bills involving the renewal of a patent that has lapsed come before the attention of the Private Bills Committee, they should be submitted to the department which has charge of such matters, and that the department should have some supervision over these applications. Otherwise we may eventually drift into this position that whenever negligence of the slightest character can be alleged the person whose patent has lapsed can come to parliament and have it renewed. I have urged before when these matters have come to the attention of the Committee of the Whole House that some fixed principle should be adopted according to which these patents should be renewed or not renewed as the case may be. I do not think it will do to continue the system of letting any negligence, however slight, or any circumstance, however trivial, be regarded as sufficient. It seems to me that if no principle has yet been laid down (and I am not aware of any), it is about time that some principle should be adopted so that persons who obtain patents and permit them to lapse will know exactly what they will have to face when they come here asking for legislation.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext:
The other night, when I presume the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) was not present, we had a case of this kind, and I then said that I have personally always objected to the renewal of these patents. At the same time the Private Bills Committee and parliament for ten years back have been accepting this principle of the renewal of patents which have lapsed in this way. The Private Bills Committee is charged with the examination of details in each particular case. The deputy commissioner of patents always attends that committee and looks into the matter on the part of the department. I am not a member of the committee and so am not in the habit of attending its meetings. The deputy commissioner always reports to me if there is anything in connection with a Bill contrary to the workings of the department. When he has not so re-

ported I have taken it for granted that the Private Bills Committee have acted in accordance with these principles, and have satisfied themselves with regard to the details. If the deputy commissioner reports to me that there is anything in connection with the Bill contrary to the practice of the department, I inform myself in regard to the Bill and am prepared to discuss it when the report of the Private Bills Committee comes before the House.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: I had occasion lately to look into this question as to the practice and the law with regard to patents in Canada, more particularly in reference to this question of the renewal of patents where through some inadvertence on the part of their owners the conditions of the Patent Act have not been complied with, and I submit to the minister that the present position of the law in this respect is very unsatisfactory. I do not think a committee of this House is a proper tribunal to inquire into these questions. I think the practice adopted in England under the Act of 1907 is much better. By that Act, under carefully drawn legislation, powers are conferred on the commissioner of patents to make full inquiries as to the circumstances of alleged inadvertence after due notice not only to those who might be affected directly or might have filed caveats, but also to the public generally through advertisements. As it is, quite frequently, we find, in reference to these Bills, that the patentees who have not complied with the provisions of the law with regard to the manufacture of their articles within the time provided by the statute are also in default with regard to the rules and, upon some specious plea as to the carelessness of their clerk, or counsel, or something of that kind, they impose upon the good nature of the committee, or perhaps the committee has not had its attention fully called by the private interests that are affected, as to the full effect of the Bill submitted, and the renewal goes through. We are reaching a stage in Canada where we should have more attention paid to the matter of our patents. The course adopted by the imperial parliament of stringently enforcing the law with regard to the manufacturing clause is one which has created a great deal of satisfaction in that country and has obtained the approval of business men in this country as well. I think that the minister ought to take the power which has been given to the commissioner of patents in England to make an inquiry into all the circumstances to ascertain whether there has been any inadvertence or overlooking of the conditions in reference to the payment of the fees or otherwise. That power is one which should be exercised by the commissioner after full investigation and not one which should be left to a committee of this House.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: I do not know that I can quite agree with the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Macdonald) as to increasing the quantity of machinery. I think is is more a matter of getting the machinery we have at work.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: I do not propose to increase the machinery, but I suppose that the provisions of the law which exist in England should be applied in this country.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext:
I understand that the hon. gentleman proposed that the people who had charge of this matter should be given a power they do not possess at the present time. I submit to the minister that there is a duty cast upon him, not merely of bringing this kind of negative evidence before the committee from time to time that he has not heard of any objection, but as the Minister cannot probably attend the meetings of the committee and has to send a deputy or subordinate to watch the interests of the public, it is absolutely necessary for the minister to see to it that from time to time he has a report of the actual circumstances attending the proposed renewal and that he should inquire into these circumstances and see if they are such as commend themselves to his judgement, so that he can come before this committee and tell it that his opinion is that the renewal should or should not be sanctioned by this committee. It is not sufficient to my mind, for the minister to come before us and plead that he has heard no objection, non constat, the deputy may have forgotten all about it, or he may have very little judgment in regard to the matter. But, we are getting away from the principle of responsible government when the Minister does not take this matter in hand and gradually formulate a rule which shall guide him in all cases, so that, as each case arises, he will have precedents to go by or analogies to consult and be able to say that it is right that this should be granted or that it should not be granted. The minister has said that he is opposed to this indiscriminate renewal, but it goes on all the same. We have no knowledge of whether this patent has been put into actual use or not, whether the parties have been exercising their rights or not, and we have just this mistake of law put forward as a reason why the renewal was not obtained at the proper time. Does the minister think that a mistake of law is a proper ground upon which a renewal should be granted? It is very doubtful whether such a reason should be accepted. I do not think a private Bills committee is the best possible tribunal to decide a question of that kind. I think the minister should have a policy upon the matter. He has

legal officers in his department and he should be prepared to say that he has come to the conclusion that he should or should not consent to a renewal of the patent on the mere excuse that the patentee has misunderstood the law. Generally speaking, courts of justice have found that there is a no more dangerous kind of excuse than the excuse of misunderstanding the law. Every man is bound to know the law. It is pretty hard to know it sometimes, I admit, but that is the principle we adopt in the courts of justice. In this case the minister does not take any responsibility in regard to it, and on the ground of misunderstanding what the law was the plea is put forward that the party allowed his time to lapse. I do not want to advance any unnecessary criticism of the minister, but I think from this time on, at all events, assuming that this government is going to control the affairs of Canada for a little while longer, we ought to have the minister take the responsibility of his position in connection with these matters and see that in each case he has some knowledge of the circumstances attending it before it comes before the committee and be able to advise the committee as to what is the proper course to pursue.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext:
I may say as chairman of the Private Bills Committee, in answer to the question asked by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), that the committee, for nearly ten years has pursued its present policy in regard to the revival of expired patents. Where good grounds were presented a failure to comply with the law for one year has not been regarded as a bar to the renewal of the patent. This principle has been applied to the special case now before us. This company had their patent for six years ; less than one year has been allowed to elapse since the time at which the patent should be renewed. Good grounds have been advanced for the neglect to renew the patent. They gave good reasons why the licensee did not renew his patent in time and they showed that the right which had been acquired by other parties had in the meantime been protected. Three applications came before the committee this year in regard to which it was obvious that there had been negligence on the part of the patentee in failing to renew his patent and they were refused. But in the case of Montgomery Grey, the first six year period during which the license was in force expired on October 28, 1908. The patent is granted for eighteen years and it is necessary for the licensee to renew his patent every six years. By an inadvertence the lawyer of this patentee Montgomery Grey, overlooked the 28th of October which was the last day for renewing Mr. LENNOX.
the patent for the next six years. These parties have taken steps to protect the acquired rights of other parties. The commissioner of patents has always attended the meetings of the Private Bills Committee when Bills relating to patents have come before that committee. But, in answer to the hon. member for South Sim-coe (Mr. Lennox), I would say that I think the law should be amended. As it is now, the only way to protect the licensee who may have good grounds to ask for a renewal of his patent is to come before the House and obtain it by means of a private Bill. I think the general law with regard to patents should be amended giving the necessary powers to the commissioner to inquire into these cases. This would save a great deal of trouble, and the department and the government could attend to these cases in a more careful and satisfactory manner than is at present possible.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: There are two matters of general interest, apart from this Bill, which have been brought up, and I would like to say a word or two upon them. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has suggested that the power of renewing expired or lapsed patents should be vested in the commissioner of patents and that private Bills should not necessarily be brought before parliament for that purpose. I may say to my hon. friend-I am not sure whether he was in the House at the time or not-that some years ago, when I was making several amendments to the Patent Act, that point was thoroughly discussed, and parliament objected to divesting itself of the power to deal with these lapsed patents and objected to giving that power to the commissioner of patents. I am not anxious to have that power. I would be willing to assume it if parliament desired to impose it upon the department, but I do not desire it at all and I would much prefer that it should not be imposed upon me, because it would involve the exercise of judicial functions of the greatest importance and in some cases it would involve millions of dollars of value in the reinstatement of patents. If that had been the intention of parliament when it amended the Patent Act I would have accepted the responsibility, but parliament decided that should not be done.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: Two years ago that principle was adopted in England.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext:
When this parliament disposed of the matter in 19U0 that regulation had not been passed by the English parliament. It is possible that if it had been the parliament of Canada might have come to a different decision from that which it did. As to a rule in dealing with the renewal of these patents, shortly after I became Minister of Agriculture I discussed

the question before the Private Bills Committee and the committee then laid down the rule that where the omission of the payment of fees appeared to be due to inadvertence or negligence on the part of the attorney rather than on the part^ of the owner of the patent, the patent might be renewed, provided always that the term during which the patent had lapsed was not too long. I do not think any definite rule as to the length of time was laid down, but the practice has been one year. In this case the patent was taken out on the 28th of October, 1902, and the fees were paid for six years which lapsed on the 28th of October, 1908, only a few months ago. That date passed probably through the inadvertence of the attorney, and the Private Bills Committee having examined the matter reported to this House in favour of the Bill. There does not seem to be anything contrary to the practice of parliament in that, and under the curcumstances I feel justified in supporting the recommendation of the Private Bills Committee. In most cases the recommendation of the Private Bills Committee has been accepted by parliament, but a good many cases no doubt have occurred in which the committee have rejected applications of this kind. The rights which have accrued during the lapsed period of the patent have always been protected by a clause similar to that which appears at the end of this Bill. I give this explanation because the impression has been conveyed that the department has been negligent of its duty in dealing with these patent bills. That is not a fair imputation on the department. I do not think it is necessary, as suggested by the hon. member for Simcoe, that a special report should be presented to parliament from the Deputy Commissioner of Patents in connection with each of these Bills; but I am quite ready to follow any expression of opinion by the House in that matter.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext: Notwithstanding the clear statement of the case made by the minister, I am inclined to agree with my hon. friend (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) that such matters as this should be dealt with by the commissioner of patents rather than by parliament. I am not a member of the Private Bills Committee, and therefore do not know what evidence may have been given as to whether this patent as a matter of law did, or did not expire on the 28th of October, 1908, but from a cursory reading of this Bill it would appear that the latter part of section 2 actually cures any defects which may have existed in this patent down to 1908. Under the Patent Act if a man fails to commence manufacture within two years from the granting of the patent his patent is void or if he has imported the patented article after one year after the granting of the patent it is also void or if he has refused the right to any person to manufacture under certain conditions prescribed by the Act, his patent is also void. I suspect that many of the Bills brought before this parliament for renewal of patents are brought because the patent has. become void under the law and so that they may be renewed by a special Act, rather than because of any neglect to pay the fees. There is something very suspicious in this very Bill we are now considering. Section 2 provides that any person who has commenced the manufacture of this article since October, 1908, may continue to do so, but that exemption is not to extend to any person who, without the consent of the holder of the patent, has commenced to use, construct, or manufacture such invention before the expiry of the letters patent. It seems to me that this Bill would rehabilitate the patent and override certain provisions in the General Patent Act with regard to the rights of others. If a person commenced to manufacture before October 28, 1908, he would have a perfect right to do so under the Patent Act, but it seems to me that the latter part of this clause takes away from him the protection which the law gave him and under it the patentee would have a right to bring an action foT infringement. I do not know enough of the particular conditions connected with this Bill to vote against it, but it seems to me there is a great deal in what the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) says, that this matter should be dealt with by the department, and that the department should have positive proof that the patent has been kept alive, and that the patentee has complied with all the conditions of the Patent Act. I believe that the Commissioner of Patents and not a committee of this House should be the judge in such a case. I suggest that the minister take this matter into serious consideration and^ before another session introduce legislation making the law more clear than it is at present regarding these extensions of patents. I suspect that in this very case there is something wrong with the patent, and that we are curing the defect by the legislation we are passing to-day.

maintopic: LETTERS PATENT OF F. M. GREY.
speechtext:
I would say to my hon. friend who has drawn attention to the last clause of the last section, that these words have not generally appeared in the clause to which I referred as being usual in the Patent Acts, and I do not think they are necessary here to safeguard any person who has commenced the manufacture or the use of the article during the lapsed period, unless there is some such object in view as my hon. friend suggests. Although the deputy minister has not reported to me that there is anything objectionable in the Bill, I think perhaps it would be as well to let it stand until we look into this matter.

What is the present condition of affairs with regard to the commercial treaty with France, and what is the cause of the delay in reference to the matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The treaty of 1907 was approved in due course by the parliament of Canada and also by the Chamber of Deputies of France, but when it reached the French Senate there was very considerable delay owing to the strong opposition among the French senators who claimed that the treaty was too favourable to Canada. After considerable delay and negotiation, a supplementary treaty was entered into, which has been laid before this House. That, as well as the original treaty, has been approved by the French Senate, but it requires yet to be approved by the Chamber of Deputies. We have delayed bringing forward a resolution to confirm the supplementary treaty because we desire to await the action of the French Chamber of Deputies. That body adjourned for several weeks, but I anticipate that at an early date the treaty will receive its approval, and at the same time steps will be taken to present to this parliament a measure for the approval of the new treaty.

["I know that after Mr. Foster left the province, it was reported outside that he had promised the tunnel at a cost of $150,000,000. But I never heard him make that statement; it was never reported in any paper in our prov ince that he had said such a thing. The Finance Minister tells us that there is 'no information.' We in that province want the tunnel; it is the most vital thing affecting our prosperity. We made a bargain with the Dominion of Canada when we entered confederation, and one of the conditions of that bargain was that the Dominion should maintain continuous communication with the mainland. That part of the bargain has not been kept. We thought we were to become part of the great Dominion and to share in its prosperity, and we depended upon this continued communication with the mainland for a very large share of that prosperity. But thirty years have elapsed, and this part of the bargain is not carried out. It is true this government has already had to pay some damages on account of the breach of that contract, and likely they will have to pay more. Two provinces, any more than two individuals, should not make a solemn bargain, signed and sealed, and then break it. Now, we want the information which the Minister of Finance says is necessary in order to justify him in promising or not promising the tunnel. We want a sum put in the estimates to make a survey to ascertain whether or not a tunnel can be built. We are not unreasonable; we will not ask for the tunnel if it is to cost $150,000,000, or half that much. We will only ask what is reasonable. In the meantime, we want to know what is possible. And we cannot get that information becausj Mr. FIELDING.
this government does not see fit to spend a few thousand dollars, or a few hundred thousand dollars if necessary, to find out whether or not this tunnel can be built. Did the Conservative administration behave in this manner? No; they started to make a survey of the Strait and spent some money on it. But the survey required some time, and the government went out of power before the work was completed. And, since this administration came into power in 1896, it has not spent a dollar in getting the information referred to by the Minister of Finance. I have quoted what the Minister of Finance said when he was in Prince Edward Island. I would like now to refer to another very prominent man on that side. In 1891, the right hon. leader of this government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) visited Prince Edward Island, and he is reported-and has never denied it- reported by a prominent Liberal politician -as reported in the papers at that time and published all over the island-as saying:
Every man who has given attention to the condition of things and the interests involved by the entering of the island into confederation must admit that such a tunnel must be constructed if the thing is reasonably practical.
Coming to the province before an election, the right hon. gentleman made this promise. Yet he has been in power for twelve years, and has never made a step to find out whether or not the work is reasonably practicable. I urge the government, with all the strength I have, to place a sum of money in the estimates and have a proper survey made of the straits so as to have this question settled, whether or not this tunnel is practicable. That is all we ask-' only this and nothing more,' or less. But I regret that this tunnel matter is not taken up properly even by all. There is a class-a small class of people in our own province who look upon it with apathy; they say they do not think we can get it, that it will cost a very large sum of money. These people do not know that about which they are speaking. No man knows whether the tunnel will cost $100,000,000 or $10,000,000. Any man who makes a statement as to the amount of money it will cost simply shows that he does not know anything about it. We shall never know what the tunnel will cost until a survey is made of the strait. I urge the government not to allow these promises that it has made and the hopes it has held out to go into the already overcrowded graveyard of their broken promises. When the Prime Minister 'finishes his work,' I hope he will not forget to finish this survey which was commenced under the Conservatives, and which has been neglected from that day to this.

Now, as to the expenditure of money, a great deal depends not alone on the amount of money expended, but the way in which it is spent. This is a young and growing country, and necessarily will require large expenditures on public works and means of transportation ana works of that kind. Nobody will condemn the government for spending this money on useful works. But what the government should be condemned for is spending money on works that are not useful and not required. This government can afford to spend a million dollars on what is called the Aylesworth ditch.
This expenditure will serve the interests only of a certain township and perhaps serve the interests of [DOT] the government in securing more support in that township. It is, however, a questionable expenditure and while the government should not be condemned for expending money usefully, it should bfe condemned when it undertakes such large expenditures which cannot be better defended than this undertaking.
There is another expenditure of a questionable character, the building of that section of the Transcontinental Railway from Quebec to Moncton. This was condemned in the House by the most prominent railroad authority of that time, the then Minister of Railroads, the late Hon. Mr. Blair. Mr. Blair said that it was an unnecessary work, that it was parallelling the Intercolonial Railway and that the construction of that road would eventually turn the Intercolonial Railway into scrap iron. Yet this government has gone on with the construction of that road at a great cost and we will have the spectacle of two government roads parallelling one another from Quebec to Moncton, when one good road would amply serve the purpose and afford railway facilities for the people in that country. At the same time other sections of the country are languishing and starving for railroads, but the government in its wisdom or unwisdom has seen fit to build this unnecessary and unjustifiable section of the National Transcontinental Railway.
The expenditure on the Militia Department is open to criticism. This is the only department whose expenditure has not been reduced this year. The department costs the country about $7,000,000 a year. To keep up what? A standing army? We have read of an army where they were all officers and no men. There is a feeling in this country that a great deal of this money is going to the officers, and yet when the time comes, if ever it should come, when there will have to be fighting by the people of this country, it will be found as it has been before, that the fighting will be done not by the men who are living in luxury and enjoying large salaries with all this fuss and feathers as the hon. member
for Nanaimo says about them, the fighting will be done by the hard working men from the country and the towns. There is a feeling of distrust with reference to this militia expenditure. I have no doubt there are many good men in the Militia Department, I have no reason for saying otherwise, but there is a feeling that there is much more spent in that department than the returns justify, and I think that perhaps a certain amount of that money might be more profitably spent in other directions.	_
Much as has been said about making a gift of a Dreadnought to Great Britain. If the government and the people saw fit to do this, I do not think any fault could be found. I think it would be better to make some such gift as that than to waste any money on the Militia Department. I am not saying all the money has been wasted, but there is a feeling that this department is doing as it likes without any check and I am not surprised that a government supporter should come out and state that there is too much fuss and feathers in that department. I firmly believe that of the $7,000,000 spent on the militia at least some has not been spent in a profitable and useful way.

In resuming this debate, I find that the discussion has been tolerably exhaustive on both sides. Consequently, it may be somewhat difficult for me to find anything novel or new to say. However, I think it is an accepted fact that no two individuals deduce exactly the same conclusions on any question, and I presume that that rule will hold good in the present instance, and that I may be enabled to say something that has not already been said. Before referring to any of the arguments or statements of our friends opposite, I wish to congratulate the Finance Minister on the very admirable and satisfactory budget deliverance which we heard on Tuesday last. I know that, in view of the falling revenue, and in view of the financial and commercial depression which has existed for some time, it was the general impression in the country that the Finance Minister would have to announce a very considerable deficit. It was also feared that he might have to announce an increase in the taxation. But we find that, instead of a deficit, there is a very substantial surplus, and that there is no increase in the taxation to be made, but, on the contrary, the government have wisely, I think, decided to decrease the expenditures and to practice the most rigid economy in order that the revenues may be sufficient to meet the requirements. It is probable that some of us may be a little disappointed because appropriations were not made for some improvements that we might consider were desirable and necessary in our several constituencies. It is probable also, that the people may be somewhat disappointed in this respect, but I am sure that, when they understand the circumstances, they will give the government credit for their good intentions. I am also sure that the country will endorse the course taken by the government in reducing the expenditure with
a view to keeping it within the revenue. I must also congratulate the Minister of Finance on his determination to continue to the manufacturers of beet-root sugar the advantages that they have enjoyed for the last few years. This is an infant industry which promises to be of very great importance and value to the people of this country and this is a species of protection, if I may use that expression, which is advantageous to both consumer and producer. It is advantageous to the consumer because it supplies additional competition in the finished product and consequently enables him to purchase that product more cheaply than he otherwise could. It is of advantage to the producer or the farmer because it creates a ready market for a new and what promises to be a profitable farm product, for it has been established beyond perad-venture that the sugar beet can be grown in Canada to very great perfection and at a very considerable profit. It has been established by experience thus far that it i3 a profitable crop for the farmer to grow. Not only that but it works in very well with other crops, and its cultivation and harvesting can be carried on at seasons of the year when other work on the farm is comparatively slack and labour is more plentiful; and as a result the root can be

the expenditure is not a criminal offence i providing we have the revenue to meet that expenditure and providing the expenditure has been fairly economical and honest. As to whether this expenditure has been honest or economical we can perhaps judge better by a comparison than in any other way. We have a government in Ontario which our good friends opposite say is honest and economical. I am not going to dispute that point because I believe it is honest and possibly fairly economical. But the expenditure under that government during the past five years has nearly doubled. I am not going to say that it has been dishonest or that the government has been recklessly extravagant because the province has enlarged. If the province has increased we must expect an additional expenditure there the same as here in the Dominion. But there is another province which I might mention and some of our friends swear by the government of that province. I refer to the government of Manitoba. They say that it is honest and economical and possibly they are right I have no figures for the province of Manitoba but I think I am correct in saying that the expenditure has a good deal more than doubled since the present government came into power. If that is the case in connection vith these other governments why should this government be blamed for an increase in the expenditure. It should not be forgotten that the expenditure has increased by $1,000,000 for the purpose of assisting the provinces of the Dominion in the form of an increased indemnity. The statement has been made and repeated several times during this discussion by our friends opposite that the taxation of the people has been doubled; or possibly that is not just the way to put it, but they say that the people have been required to pay double the taxation under the present government that they did under the late government. I am quite willing to admit that is the case. But, Sir, the rate of taxation has not been increased. The rate of taxation has been very considerably lowered. If the people, by reason of their increased prosperity, are enabled to buy double the amount of taxable goods under the present government that they were able to buy under the late government, surely no person will say that it is a cause of complaint against the present government. If, by reason of the increased prosperity of the country, due to the policy of the government, to take as an example what, I dare say, has been given many times before, I am enabled, owing to the increased wages which I receive, owing to increased prosperity in my business, or in my affairs, to purchase two suits of clothes in a year and add to my other luxuries and comforts in life, instead of one suit a year, as I 155

formerly did under the late government, surely I have reason for thankfulness and have no reason for complaint against the present government. If anything, I should have reason for complaint against those who preceded the present government and who kept me in such a position that I was only able to buy one suit of clothes.
Another complaint is that the public debt has been largely increased. We all know that that is the case but before I go on to discuss that point I want to dissent entirely from the principle which was laid down the other day by the hon. member for Ar-gentueuil (Mr. Perley) that every generation should pay the liabilities of that particular generation and should present a clean slate to the succeeding generation. Most of this money which has caused the public debt has been expended in permanent improvements-improvements that are not only good for the present day but will be advantageous to the people of many generations after this. That being the ease, why should the people of the present day be burdened in order to provide comforts and conveniences and necessities for the next two generations? If that principle were adopted and carried out it would be the means of blocking many useful and profitable enterpises. But let us see in what manner the public debt has been increased and I will just give you one instance. I could give you many. In 1896, which was the last year of the government of our friends opposite, there was an expenditure made on railways and canals of 2,699,669. In 1908 the present government expended $28,363,758. In view of these facts is it any wonder that the debt has been increased, and will any person deny that we have received value for that increase in the public debt. Why, Sir, as a result of the improvement of our water highways this country has already become the envy of our great neighbours to the south because we are carrying the trade from their doors and, to-day, trade which was formerly done through American channels is being done through Canadian channels. My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) in the course of his very able address stated that one of the great reasons for the increase of the debt under the Conservative government was that they purchased the Northwest Territories, that the purchase price had been added to the public debt, and that it was not all yet paid for. That is quite true, but my hon. friend might have gone a little bit further and he might have told this House and the people of the country that of that territory which was purchased and paid for by the money of the people no less than 25,000,000 acres of the very best land in it was given away. And not only that, but an agreement was entered into by the government with the recipients that that land should be free
from municipal taxation for a long period of years.

When the hon. gentleman states that 25,000,000 acres was given away he does not mean that there was no return obtained for that land? What was that land worth at the time the contract was made with the Canadian Pacific Railway?

There certainly was a return but I think I am safe in saying that a good many multi-millionaires have been made out of that land. And I wish to say further, that if the hon. gentleman who interrupted me, or if any others of his friends on that side of the House consider that this giving away of that land was an evidence of superior foresight or superior statesmanship, then, most people will disagree with them as to the meaning of these terms. Our friends on the other side admit that we have had very prosperous times during the regime of the present government, but they claim that all this prosperity is due to the policy which they inaugurated. Well, they had 18 long years in which to work out this great policy of theirs and year after year under their policy the country became worse and worse and the condition of the people poorer and poorer. Especially during the last three or four years of the Conservative government we had scarcity of employment, low wages, and soup kitchens in every city; we had depression in its worst form and the movement of population was from this country to the United States instead of the reverse of that as at present. In these days of the Conservative government we were losing the best blood of our country, our promising young men were leaving for the United States and we were building up the wealth and the population of a foreign nation.
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to tell us what legislation the present government has placed upon the Statute-books which has brought about this prosperity he speaks of?

Yes, I will tell the hon. gentleman that this government has used the legislation that is on the Statute-books to such better advantage than the Conservative government as to bring about these results. And further, there have been many changes made in the tariff which have tended to the better and more progressive conditions which obtain to-day. Now, during the last nine or ten years work has been abundant, wages have been high, business has been prosperous, the country has been booming. I think, and I believe the people of this country think, that if that policy can be carried out so much more to the interests of the people by the present government than by the previous government they would be foolish indeed Mr. M. Y. McLEAN.
to make any change in their Tulers. In view of these facts which I have related and many more that I could Telate, is it surprising that the people of Canada have expressed their entire satisfaction with the government and with the manner in which they have administered public affairs, not only once but twice-and they will do it a third time I believe when they have the opportunity.
I want to turn aside a little from the beaten path to say a few words on a subject which was not referred to in the admirable address of the Minister of Finance, and which I should have liked to have heard mentioned by him. I believe it is the duty of this parliament and of the government to do everything legitimately within their power to suppress, or to smash if you will, all trade combines and trusts in this country. I know of no more expeditious or more efficient way of doing this than by hewing a good big gap out of the tariff wall which surrounds them so as to permit of a liberal influx of outside or foreign competition. It may be said that this has been provided for already, and that is true to a limited extent, but only to a limited extent. We have been provided with the machine, but the motive power to operate the machine has been withheld. There is a clause in the Customs Act which says that when it is proven to the satisfaction of some legal tribunal that a combine exists, the government have the power to reduce or to entirely remove the customs duties on the products of any such combine. But the duty of hunting up evidence and of conducting the prosecution is left to a private individual. I maintain that parliament, at the instance of the government of course, having enacted the tariff law, it is their duty to protect the public from all abuses which may arise under that law. While the exactions of these combines or trusts are very large in the aggregate, they are comparatively small to the individual, and hence it is not worth the while of the individual to go to the expense of seeking evidence and conducting a prosecution against them. The result is that the combines are allowed to go on from day to day, growing in strength and power, and, if I might be allowed to use the expression, in impudence. As an illustration, I am just as sure as I am standing here at this moment that a combine exists among the paper manufacturers of this country. You may apply to a dozen different paper manufacturers and you will get precisely the same quotation from each; you will receive from any one only such advantages or privileges as others will grant; you have to pay your money and take what you get, good or bad, and be thankful for it. I have seen the statement made, and not refuted, that the paper manu-

facturers of this country arc selling paper in the United States at a lower price than they are selling it at to their customers in this country. I am also informed on excellent - authority that you can import paper, what is known as news print, from Chicago laid down in Toronto, plus the freight and the duty, at just about the same price that you have to pay to the manufacturers of this [DOT] country, showing that the whole of the duty goes into the pockets of the manufacturers instead of any portion of it going into the treasury of the country. Now, although I am perfectly convinced of this, and although the exactions of this so-called combine are very large in the aggregate, yet it is not worth my while, for all it amounts to me, to search for the evidence and conduct a prosecution in order to prove the existence of that combine. What I say is that this law should be treated just as are other laws-the customs law and the excise law, for example. Officers should be appointed under the government whose duty it would be to ascertain where any combine existed and look up the evidence and conduct the prosecution. If a man attempts to bring foreign goods into this country, though it may be only a silk handkerchief, without paying duty, he is met at the frontier by a customs officer; his goods are confiscated, and possibly he is fined and punished. The same is true with regard to the excise law, and properly so. This is necessary in order to protect the revenue of this country. But surely it is as important to protect the interests of the great consuming masses of this country as it is to protect the public revenues. I use the case of the paper manufacturers, not as implying that theirs is the only combination that exists in this country, because I believe there are many such. I use this case as an illustration simply because I am more acquainted with that line of business than any other.
It has been said that we could take advantage of the Criminal Code in order to stamp out these combinations in trade. Well, that has been tried in this country in three or four instances, and I am sorry to say that it has proved a disappointment, a miserable failure, largely because of the apparent indifference of the legal authorities and the long delays that are possible under the law. I may also say that there is: a very strong feeling in the minds of a great many peoDle that the springs of justice are tempered with very great mercy towards these combines.
In conclusion, I wish, as a friend and supporter of this government, to urge them with all the earnestness that I can command, to take this matter in hand, and at once; and if the remedy I suggest is not the best remedy, then let them apply what may in their wisdom be considered the 1551
best remedy in order to stamp out this evil;
because every day these combines are allowed to continue they are growing in strength and influence. We have had an example of that in the neighbouring republic, where the combination have grown so strong that they really master the people and set parliament and the governmnet at defiance, and even the courts are afraid to touch them very strongly. If such a state of things should every unfortunately occur in this country, God help the people of the country. Again I urge upon my friends to use their utmost endeavours to free the people of this country from the tentacles of such an octupus as these combines.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the speech of the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McLean), which is a severe criticism of several of the departments of the government. I can heartily endorse what he says with regard to the combines; and if these combines exist in this country, it is certainly up to the government to take some definite action with regard to them. The hon. member gave us a great many excuses for the enormous expenditure of this country; but he did not tell us of some expenditures which have been going on in his own riding under his very nose and encouraged by him, such as the expenditure on a wharf at a place called St. Joseph's, where the whole town was sold last year for $700 of taxes.
I have had nothing to do with that expenditure. It has been supported by every representative of that constituency, including the late representative. .

I am glad to hear the hon. member say that he has had nothing to do with the expenditure on that wharf; but why did he allow the government to gd on spending money there year after year, even within the last year, since he has been a member of this House? If he will turn up 'Hansard', he will find that the Minister of Public Works, in reply to questions I asked, distinctly stated the amounts of money expended on that wharf during the last few years. I know that the previous representative of that riding condemned the expenditure on St. Joseph's wharf.
There has been no expenditure authorized since I became member. There was some expenditure authorized shortly before that, and any work done since has been to complete.

The hon. gentleman has just substantiated the statement which I made. He says that the government have

been spending money there merely to complete the work started years ago. I do not want to go into details, but the hon. gentleman knows that the original contract was practically closed and the wharf partly swept away.
I saw the wharf last year and not a foot of it was swept away. There is not a more substantial, better constructed work in Canada.

If the hon. gentleman only saw the wharf last year, he does not know the portion swept away. I have visited that wharf myself and have seen portions scattered down along the shores of Lake Huron. The hon. member knows well that large parts of the wharf were swept away.
I do not.

Some years back. If he is satisfied with this work at a cost of $20,000 of the people's money, he is prepared to support this government in anything they may do. Let me call his attention to another wharf, a wharf built at the corner of his own riding, at Grand Bend That wharf cost $25,000, and has to be kept continually in repairs. Years ago, the government thought they had completed it, but they built it on top of the sand, and the waters of Lake Huron undermined it, and the government have been spending hundreds and thousands of dollars to repair the top part.
There never was $100,000 spent on that wharf altogether.

but you have to educate the people there to consume the products we produce in this country before you can export to them in _ any great quantity. One is struck with the enormous quantity of products that Great Britain has taken from us and the very small proportion of our exports that went to Germany. Yet if I understand the hon. gentleman his position is that we are to withdraw the preference from that country which is taking 60 per cent of our great agricultural productions in order to conciliate Germany which imports $2,000,000,000 worth and put us upon its maximum tariff because we gave the preference to Great Britain. Does the hon. member want the British preference repealed?

This is an old question, a hardy annual; you can expect it every year. I asked the hon. minister a question. Does he not realize that we are practically compelled to send the goods that we send to Great Britain there because we cannot send them anywhere else? Can we send them to the United States, a country that exported $250,000,000 worth of just such products as we are exporting to Great Britain? Can we send them to Russia?
The hon. member asks me a question, I answer yes. He says we have sent 60 per cent to Great Britain. There is 40 per cent more of that market, we can work on that. .

If the hon. gentleman will look back a few years, he will find that we were sending these goods there long before he took the office he now holds.
Mr. ARMSTRONG
Not in such quantities.

If the hon. gentleman remembers his own statements he will recall that he said distinctly on the platforms of this country that he was going to give to the people of Canada the market to the south of us, a market of 85,000,000. He told us he was going to open up the markets of the world to the farmers of Canada. Has he done it? No, he has done the opposite, he has practically sealed the second best market in the world and now he is hiding behind the preference. I would like him to tell the people of one advantage that the preference has been to the farmers or people of Canada. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) stated the other day that the preference was a far-sighted policy, as regards the development of Canada, in that it affords us access into the best market of the world, the British market for our ever-increasing agricultural products. He knows full well that we have access into the British market on exactly the same footing as any other nation.
Better.

The hon. gentleman last session tried to make us believe that the Canadian farmer was receiving more for the product of his farm on the British market because of the preference. I defy him now and have defied him time and again to show where the British consumer pays one cent more for the products of Canada than he pays for the products of Australia, New Zealand, Russia or any other country. The hon. gentleman knows full well tnat the preference does not bring us

back one penny in increased value of the products of the farm.
I hope the hon. gentleman does not assume that I am assenting to that?

He knows that by granting the preference to Great Britain he has driven us out of the German market and where are we going to be in a few years' time? The late member for Lisgar stated that the little province of Manitoba, with 73,000 square miles, was capable of producing 500,000,000 bushels of grain. When the other two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan with 250,000 square miles of land come to produce 500,000,000 bushels where are you going to send it? _ How much is Great Britain taking? How is her consumption increasing? If you examine the figures for the last five years you will find that her consumption is diminishing. That may seem a strange statement but hon. gentlemen will find that it is true. Instead of the consumption in the British market of the products of the farms of the Dominion of Canada increasing it is decreasing. Great Britain only takes 93,000,000 cwts. of wheat from all countries. Where will we be with the markets of the world closed to us	as they will be? I
would ask the minister how we are going to get rid of our products? The Minister of Customs knows full well that if we continue in the blundering mismanagement of our treaties and our trade relations with some of these countries, we will he placed in one of the most humiliating positions you can imagine any nation to be in. The hon. minister says we have 60 per cent of the British market now, what better do you want, why do you. not get the other 40 per cent? The hon. gentleman knows that if the Argentine Republic which sent $106,000,000 worth of farm products to Germany last year could sell these goods on the British market to greater advantage than on the German market she would send them to Britain. When the minister argues that having control of 60 per cent of any market we should go on and get control of 100 per cent before getting into any other market, I claim that he is not fair to the Canadian producer. The hon. gentleman knows that the ships that are going out carrying the products of Great Britain to these foreign lands must bring back loads and he may depend on it that the goods which they bring back from foreign countris are sold on the British market in competition with our goods and that you cannot, it is not reasonable to expect to get 90 per cent of any market.
When the hon. member quoted the German returns he gave the quantities and values of grain; had he figured out how much per bushel these different grains would bring?

I have not reduced it to prices per bushel. I was most careful in gathering these statistics to have them accurate. I spent some time with the Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I am indebted to him for a great deal of assistance in compiling them.	.

In making a mental calculation as the hon. member proceeded, it appeared to me that the barley, for instance, would bring about 40 cents a bushel laid down in Germany. That would not be considered a large price to the Canadian, after he had paid thte freight and the duty, and so the German market would not appear to be a valuable one for him. I would like to know what it would be worth a bushel.
It would be worth more than forty cents a bushel.
About that.
I have not figured the price per bushel.
Would it be any bonanza for the farmer to sell his barley for forty cents a bushel, pay his freight across the ocean and pay the duty to get into the German market? Can he not do better than that?
That is a very poor argument for the hon. gentleman to advance.
No, I think it is a good one. I want to know what the value of the market is.

Germany is a large consumer of barley. She imported 96,000,000 bushels of barley and paid for it $67,000,000. Does the hon. gentleman seem to think that it was a good argument to say that we should not have access to the German market? He says that barley is forty cents a bushel. I have seen the time, when, on the farms of Ontario, we were glad enough to get forty cents a bushel.
But that is less the freight-

That cannot amount to very much.

tariff.
Do I understand from the Minister of Customs that he is not anxious that we should get into the German market at all?
I want to know what the value of it is, to see if it is worth our while to sacrifice the British preference for it.

I have tried to show the Minister of Customs that Germany imported $56,000,000 worth of horses, 96,000,000 bushels of barley, 41,000,000 bushels of oats, 25,000,000 bushels of rye, 73,000,000 bushels of wheat, and I might go on down through the list. The trouble in gathering these figures is that they are given in kilos, marks and pesos; so that it requires a great deal of figuring to ascertain quantities and values. I have chosen a number of the most prominent products of the farm and I am trying to show that Germany imported last year over $300,000,000 worth of agricultural products, such as we are producing, and that we were only able to get into the German market $500,000 worth owing to the mismanagement of our trade relations with Germany by the present government.
My hon. friend has not demonstrated that we have done anything that excludes us from that market.

The Minister of Customs knows full well what he has done. No man knows better, and I venture to say that if the minister investigates these figures he will satisfy himself that it is time we opened up our trade relations with Germany.
What did we do to Germany?

There are a number of new members in this House and I have no objection to stating what the hon. gentleman did do to Germany. I will tell it in just as few words as I can. We were a favoured nation in the eyes of Germany in 1896. Our goods were going into Germany under the most favoured nation clause, or under the lowest possible tariff. The government came into power and in the first budget that he brought down the Finance Minister granted a preference to Great Britain of 12i per cent. When that 12i per cent preference was granted Sir Charles Tupper rose and stated distinctly that they would have to include Germany in the treaty. The Finance Minister rather pooh-poohed that proposition. But before a year elapsed we found him asking Great Britain to denounce the treaty between Great Britain and Germany. Great Britain did denounce the treaty between Great Britain and Germany as it then was as far as Canada was concerned, but Great Britain took mighty good care to see that she looked after herself and all the other colonies, because I want to tell you that Great Britain and all the other colonies are to-day sending their goods into Germany under the most favoured nation clause, while Canada not only has the maximum tariff against her to-day, but she has the surtax placed on top of it. What else did these hon. gentlemen do? In 1898 they increased the preference to 25 per cent. Germany said:	If.

that is the way Canada is going to treat us, if he is going to slap us in the face, we will put her under the maximum tariff. The Tesult is that to-day Canada comes under the maximum tariff. In 1900 this government raised the preference to Great Britain to 33.1 per cent. Germany said: They are determined to still slap us in the face and we will place the surtax upon Canadian goods coming into our country. Germany placed upon her statute-book a provision for the collection of the surtax, but she did not apply that surtax until one or two years afterwards and then this government applied the surtax to German goods coming into this country. The agricultural products that were going into Germany from Canada continued to go into Germany under the favoured nation clause until the last year or two, and it is only quite recently to some of these products that Germany has applied the surtax. There is the whole position, and yet hon. gentlemen opposite will tell us that the British preference that they granted to Great Britain has been the means of giving to the farmers of this country a wonderful advantage. I have not the time to go into the question to-day, but the hon. gentleman knows full well that a large portion of the goods coming into this country under the British preference comes through the middlemen to Great Britain, and that these goods are the product of foreign countries. No one knows that better than the minister himself. I would like to show the position that this government occupies with regard to the preferential tariff, but I have not the time. I want to impress upon this House the importance of getting into the German market with the products of the farms of this country, and the sooner we get in there the better it will be for the Dominion. You can depend upon it that it will take years to develop a market in Germany even after we get in there. If you look into the figures relating to the products that other countries are sending into Germany you cannot help but feel humiliated to find that Canada is sending so little.
The Minister of Customs interrupted my hon. friend from East Lamb-ton by saying that the 96,000,000 bushels of barley imported by Germany were valued at only forty cents a bushel.
Well, Toughly.
If my hon. friend will make the calculation he will find that this barley was valued at sixty cents a bushel instead of forty cents. That makes a considerable difference.

At sixty cents a bushel for Canadian barley, paying freight across the ocean and paying the minimum duty in Germany, will the hon. gentleman tell me

how much that will bring you? Will it bring 35 cents a bushel net?
That is similar to the statement made by the minister a short time ago. He then said it was forty cents a bushel, and now he admits that it was sixty cents a bushel.
You agreed with that.
I could not stop to figure it out.
