Eighty per cent on this side voted for my motion, and absolutely every Liberal, including the members from the west, voted against it.

It is a striking comment on the interest taken by the hon. gentleman's friends in this important matter, that when we look up the vote on it, we find that there were but 22 who supported the hon. gentleman. That surely shows a deplorable lack of interest on the part of his political friends in this House, and so far as his leader is concerned, he knows that he was one of those who voted against the resolution.
Better read what he said.

I assure my hon. friend I have read it. In the recent election con-157
test, this question of the tariff played a very important part in many of the constituencies of western Canada. I do not see the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. McCarthy) in his seat, but the hon. gentleman was very much exercised, during his contest, over certain statements to the effect that he had shirked his duty in connection with this resolution. On looking up the files of the Calgary newspapers, I find that on the 21st of October, the hon. gentleman offered to bet the Liberal newspaper of Calgary the 'Albertan' $100 to be donated to any hospital, if they could prove that he had shirked his duty and -had not voted on this question. The hon. gentleman realized very well what the sentiment of his constituency was in that respect, yet the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) tells us that he is a protectionist. In connection with that same resolution, let me point to this fact, that while only 78 votes altogether were cast upon it, on another amendment submitted by the leader of the opposition on the same evening-very much later in the evening-when one would naturally suppose there would be still fewer members in the House-what do we find? We find that 120 members voted for the amendment of the leader of the opposition. That resolution of the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) was one that, if the government could have seen its way clear to accept it, would have been very acceptable to the people of western Canada. But, when these matters are brought before this House, we want them treated with fairness and justice; and I say that I myself, if I had been in the House at that time under the peculiar circumstances surrounding the introduction of the resolution, in all probability would have felt compelled to vote against it.
1 have exceeded the time I intended to occupy. I have only this word to say in conclusion: I believe that the people of western Canada stand to-day in support of the present government because of the fact that on the tariff question, if they have not moved as far as they ought to have moved, yet they have moved in the right direction. And I hope they will go further in the same direction when the next revision of the tariff takes place.

Mr. Speaker, at this late hour I do not wish to take up the time of the House at great length. But, when a candidate in an election presents his views and makes promises to the people of what he will do, if elected, it is clearly his duty when he is honoured with a place in this House to redeem the promises thus made. We are discussing the budget of the Minister of Finance of the Dominion of Canada. As I understand that hon. gentleman's (Mr. Fielding) statement, the revenue of this country last year was eighty-four and a half millions, the



expenditures eighty-three millions, leaving a surplus of one and a half millions. But I understand the hon. gentleman to tell us also that the debt has increased by forty-six millions. To the uninitated, it hardly looks as if we have a surplus when we go further into debt to the extent of forty-six millions, particularly when we find that such items as bounties on steel and iron amounting to $3,200,000, and expenditure for rifles for the militia, $1,300,000, have not been charged to current expenditure. Had these items been charged to current expenditure, as would surely be most reasonable, we should have a deficit instead of a surplus. I regret that the government have not manifested greater care in the expenditure of public money. Had they done so, we might have had an actual surplus instead of a surplus that, in my opinion, exists only on paper.
I regret that the Minister of Finance in his budget has not announced that he will give protection to a certain class of people in this country, the farmers, market gardeners and labourers. As I understand the national policy enunciated by Sir John Macdonald in 1878, it is a protection first to the agriculturists and manufacturers, but also to the labourers, in fact to every class. The manufacturers of this country are fairly well protected-in some lines, probably, too highly protected, though I have no quarrel with the government on that score. But when the manufacturers are protected, I think we should protect the agriculturists, the market gardeners and labourers as well. We are living in a country which has not so early a spring as the country to the south of us. The Finance Minister has been urged to consider the granting of protection on market garden products coming into Canada. It is hardly to be expected that Canada can compete at all seasons with a country situated like the_United States. By the time the Canadian products are coming on the market, the price of the second-class stuff coming from the United States is low, and this material comes into competition with the Canadian product. What the market gardeners and farmers of this country want particularly is a specific duty on these products, not an ad valorem duty, because that is not of much use at the time of the year when protection is most needed. I do not wish to go into this matter at length, but I have a letter here from which, perhaps, I may be permitted to read a part, as it states the need better than I could state it:
The Ontario Vegetable Growers' Association ask that the customs tariff on vegetables be made specifio instead of ad valorem, which we believe would prevent our markets from becoming a dumping ground for culls, as they are at present. We would advise a specific duty equal to 30 per cent on a fair cost of production on market value of average quality on vegetables imported, which would I Mr. WALLACE.
not deter the importation of vegetables at times of scarcity or when the Canadian grower cannot supply the demand ; the market price being high at such times, the specific duty would be smaller relatively.
A specific duty would prevent our market from being flooded with the surplus or damaged products of other countries sent here at a low valuation, at a time when Canadian growers are prepared to supply an abundance of fresh home-grown products. At the same time it would improve conditions for the Canadian consumer by improving the quality of the goods imported.
We also wish to draw your attention to the fact that a very large part of Californian grown vegetables imported into Canada are produced by Chinese labour. Especially is this the case with celery, practically all of which is grown by them, and the low prices at which it can be invoiced at point of shipment is largely determined by that fact.
The parliament of Canada having imposed, and we believe wisely so, a tax of $500 on this class entering this Dominion, as a protection to Canadian labour, it appears to us unfair that the product of such coolie labour should enter into competition with the product of the Canadian vegetable grower, and by an ad valorem duty evade the protection which our laws are intended to afford. We would ask that the following duty be imposed on the vegetables mentioned.
Cabbages	2 cents per head.
Celery	20 cents per dozen.
Onions	20 cents per bushel of 50 lbs.
In the arrangement of our duties, it is clearly wise for us to take into consideration the fact that Canada is a northern country. We should allow for the fact also that Canada is a young country, one whose industries are not fully developed, and whose population is not large. The agriculturists, market gardeners and labourers are certainly deserving of consideration. We have imported within the last few years hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of these market garden goods from the United States nearly all of which should be grown in the Dominion. Such articles, when demanded before their season, are clearly a luxury, not a necessity. Such a duty therefore, is a luxury and would not affect the poor, and the rich the only ones whom it would affect, can afford to pay a little more for the benefit of a class of producers who should be encouraged. I hope the government will take that into their serious consideration, and that the Minister of Agriculture will do something for the market gardeners. The deputation that waited on him and the Minister of Finance asked that when seeds are r>ut up in packages the percentage of germination be printed on the packages, as thousands of dollars are lost every year through the use of worthless seeds and nobody is made responsible for that loss.
I regret that the government did not see their way clear to place a higher duty

on hogs and hog products entering Canada, as the present duty is not sufficiently laTge to prevent the fluctuations of price in hogs in the United States affecting the price of hogs in Canada, and therefore it is the duty of the government to place a sufficient protection to prevent our market from being made a slaughter market for American hogs. The government has been giving a great deal of protection to manufacturers, and they should seriously consider helping out the farmers to the moderate extent asked by these deputations.
During the election campaign one of my planks against the Dominion government was their system of immigration. _ Much of the immigration coming into this country, I believe, is not in the public interest. This subject has been thoroughly discussed in the House. I think we should encourage, as we are encouraging, men from the old land, men from different parts of Europe who make good settlers and men from the United States who are coming in in thousands, but I do not think we have any room for the class of people who come to Canada but never become good Canadians or British subjects. We want people who will come in and make good citizens in time to come. The immigration of Japanese and Doukhobors and people of that class should be either restricted or not encouraged. I have listened with a great deal of attention to members on both sides of the House during the budget debate, and it is only fair to say that I agree heartily with some things said on both sides. I noted particularly that nearly every man speaking on the government side goes in to defend nearly everything the government has done. The government of this country is certainly not perfect, and a man who defends all its acts must defend some things which are wrong. I was rather amused at the member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) who, in making a very able, eloquent and well studied speech defended the government in everything they had done from 1896 down until he struck what is known as the Newmarket canal. Before I came here I concluded from my own belief and knowledge that the construction of the Newmarket canal was a useless waste of public money. After listening to the defence of that project by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Railways, I was sure I was right in that conclusion because their defence was no defence at all. The Prime Minister said that the reason for building a canal and spending one or two millions of dollars on it was tliat a delegation came down from North York to ask the government to do it. Why, I could get a deputation from any part of Canada to come down and ask the government to spend one or two millions near a village, but that is no reason for spending the money. Another 157i
point about that expenditure was that $30,000 or $40,000 was spent before the delegation came down here, and yet we are led to believe that the government started that canal because the deputation came here. That was hardly fair, and I do not think it was intentional. There was no expenditure on the canal for four years except some $31,000 up to March 31, 1908, but from that date to the present about $182,000 have been spent on it. It looked to any one who studied the question at all as if this -expenditure was intended as a bribe to the electors of North York, spending $182,000 in a constituency just before an election.
I do not think that any hon. member, no matter to what political party he belongs, should support expenditures of that kind.
I condemned that expenditure on the platform in Centre York and once or twice in North York, and I believe that the people of that district, although the money is being spent there, will in time reject the men who wasted public money in that way.
I do not wish to take up the time of the House at this late hour. I would simply impress upon the government the necessity of doing something for the market gardeners and farmers. I hope the government will realize that what we ask in this respect is not for the benefit of one class or for one section of the country alone but is for the good of the Dominion at large.

LOGGIE (Northumberland, New Brunswick), Mr. Speaker, you have not heard from the province of New Brunswick during this debate and therefore I wish to make a few remarks. The hon. member for Centre York (Mr. Wallace) who has just taken his seat, has _ asked that the government should restrict immigration and he refers to the Japanese as a people who should not be allowed to enter Canada to any great extent. The hon. gentleman should know that this is exactly what the government have done, that restrictions are now being enforced and that during the last year a very limited number of Japanese have come into this country. The hon. gentleman ought to know as well that the government are using every endeavour to have a proper class of immigrants come into this country, and that every precaution is taken that when undesirable immigrants are landed in this country they are returned to the place whence they came at the_ expense of the transportation company bringing them to Canada. Another plea made by the hon. gentleman who has taken his seat is that the government should increase the protection to the agricultural interest, and he cites the protection on hogs, which he says ought to be increased. Forsooth there is a duty now of two cents per pound or

four dollars per barrel, and yet the hon. gentleman wants to have the farming interests of Canada protected to a greater extent than four dollars per barrel on pork. The hogs that come into this country are very largely of a class which are not raised in Canada. The imported hog products are consumed in the maritime provinces and in the lumbering operations of Ontario and Quebec and the eastern provinces. My hon. friend would ask that those who are consumers should pay an increased tax to the farming interest of this country. In my judgment it would he unfair to the consumer to increase the taxation on that product when we realize that the producers are already protected to what I consider a sufficient extent. If there is one item in the tariff list which, it seems to me, is on a protective tariff basis, it is the item of hog products. That is one of the items which the Liberal party have continued in force which was in force under the Conservative party in 1896. As to the request of the market gardeners that they be protected, I think we will admit that the products that are imported into this country are imported at a time at which they cannot and are not supplied by our Canadian market gardeners. If that be true is it reasonable that the consumers should be unduly taxed? They are reasonably taxed now? They pay what is a fair tax for revenue purposes. I think that the government have acted wisely in not every year tinkering with the tariff and making changes. We have framed a new tariff about each decade, and during the interim changes of no great consequence have been made. I do not think that I need refer any more to the remarks by the hon. gentleman. But, I want once again to congratulate my hon. friend the Minister of Finance on the showing that he has brought down to this House. A year ago he told the House and the country that it was a time for caution and that yet we should take courage. It seems to me, from the report laid on the table by the Minister of Finance, _ that this is exactly what the Finance Minister has done.
The hon. member for Centre York (Mr. Wallace) tells us that the expenditure was $83,000,000, that the revenue was $84,500,000 and that we have a surplus of $1,500,000. It is certainly an encouraging fact that it is so because of the stress, if I may so term it, it might have been fair to expect that the Finance Minister would come down to the House showing a deficit on the year's transactions. I think, therefore, that we might repeat what was said a year ago that perhaps no Finance Minister has ever done more to sustain the high credit of the country than has the present Minister of Finance. From his statement we find that the estimated net debt of the country on the 31st March, 1909, was upwards of $323,000,-Mr. LOGGIE.
000, and that during the twelve and three-quarter years, since 1896, we have added to the net debt, in round numbers, $65,000,000. But, Mr. Speaker, I want you to mark that the $65,000,000 is accounted for by $52,500,000 expended on the Transcontinental Railway. That leaves a balance of only $12,000,000 expended on the great public works of this country which would represent about $1,000,000 each year for the twelve years. Will you just recall to mind what has happened during the last five years of the Conservative regime? During that five years they expended $16,000,000 on capital account. During the very same term they borrowed $21,000,000: that is to say they had not sufficient money in the treasury to pay the ordinary running expenses of the country. They had to borrow $5,000,000 for that purpose. But the Liberal party have expended about $100,000,000 annually on ordinary consolidated account and the other great public works that they have undertaken during the past twelve years, have added to the public debt only $1,000,000 per annum over and above the expenditure on the National Transcontinental Railway. It seems that the situation is one from which we might well take courage and which should warrant us in going on and completing this great undertaking. We find that in the year 1896, when the Conservative party gave up the reins of power the per capita debt was $50.82, while in 1909, after we had expended $52,500,000 on the Transcontinental Railway, and after the expenditure on other great public works, we have reduced the per capita to $45.72, equal to a decrease in the debt of the country after all these great expenditures of about 10 per cent. I mean the per capita debt, of course. I have explained already that the net debt has been increased, but we have assets for it as I shall tell you later on. Now, I want to say a word about how we got this money. Perhaps I should remind the House here that the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) in speaking of that the other day used the following language:

which surpluses were got absolutely and
solely because of extraordinary taxing powers that the government availed themselves of. If the government had kept the volume and burden of taxation down to what it was, or to anything near what it was, in Liberal Conservatives times, they could not have amassed such immense sums of money, and they could not have had such large surpluses. If a government will tax sufficiently, it will have large revenue and may have large surpluses.
Now, Mr. Speaker, during the last five years of the Conservative regime, they taxed at the rate of about 14 per cent more than the present administration is taxing. Let me put it in this way. In 1908 we collected 16 -48 per cent on $351,879,000 worth of imports. In 1896 there were imports valued at $105,-

361,000 and the rate collected in that year was 19 -12 per cent. Our rate is $2.74 on the $100 less on the value of the invoice, or equal to a difference of about 12i per cent on the duty collected. Apply this and it would demonstrate that if in 1896, under the Conservative government, the people of Canada had imported as many goods as they did last year under the Liberal regime, the Conservative government would have taken out of the pockets of the people over $9,000,000 in extra taxation. If, on the other hand, last year the Liberal government had exacted the same rate of duty as did the Conservative government before 1896, there would have been $9,000,000 more collected in duties, and then our surplus would be ten and a half million dollars instead of one and a half millions. But, the hon. gentleman from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), and the hon. gentleman from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) say that the vital point is that the present government collects $11 per head, whereas in 1896 the Conservative government collected only $5.46 per head. My contention is that the vital point is the rate at which $11 per head was collected. If I pay taxes on $10,000 this year at two per cent, and I am fortunate enough next year to have $20,000 on which to pay taxes at li per cent, I pay a less rate but I pay more money on the whole and I ought to be glad I am able to pay it because I have something to represent the extra payment. And why is it that at a less rate of duty than formerly, there is more revenue produced? The answer is perfectly simple. A merchant will keep in his store just the goods his customers require, and if there is a demand for two suits of clothes now where there was only a demand for one suit before, the merchant will have the two suits and the customer will buy them instead of one.
Why not manufacture them here and pay no duty?
Oh my dear man, don't you know we do manufacture them here? Let me tell my hon. friend that there is a very small proportion of clothing imported into this country.
The house doing the largest business in the province of Ontario imports all their ready-made clothing under this tariff.

I will accept the hon. gentleman's word but I can tell him that I know of not one but of dozens of mercantile establishments that do not import one dollar's worth of ready-made clothing. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) advanced an argument the other day which it would have been fairer for him to have carried out to its logical conclusions. He told us that in 1886 we would
find $10,000,000 charged to capital account but that was for seven and a half million acres of land, which, as an asset, converted into money was worth $22,500,000, and he asked us to take that into consideration. Well, I will admit the hon. gentleman's argument, but had he been fair he would have carried it further and he would have explained that the fifty-two and a half million dollars spent on the National Transcontinental Railway was a national asset. Will the hon. gentleman have the audacity to tell me that in the National Transcontinental Railway we have not an asset representing that fifty two and a half millions. Does he not know very well that in a short time that money will be bearing interest and and that it is just as if we got the fifty-two and a half millions back, put it in the bank, and drew our interest on it, as in the ease of the twenty-two and a half million dollars we received for the public lands. Is not that a fair comparison to make? Then, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) spoke about borrowing during the interim, ' but that argument was answered by the Minister of Finance who told us that it was a temporary loan which had been paid oil. if the manager of an ordinary mercantile establishment borrows during the year and pays off his debt, he has no explanation to make to his directors. What he has to explain to the directors is what he owes and what he has to represent it. Then, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) also insinuated that if the Minister of Finance had taken care of the surpluses it would not have been necessary for him to go to the London markets to borrow money. I would point out to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) that no one can deny that the moneys received by the government have been wisely expended, for, although there may have been some small items here and there that might not be expended as we all would like, yet on the whole there is not a man on the opposite side of the House who would undertake to charge that there has been any improper expenditure of public money. It is all very well to make insinuations and inuendo, but when it comes to making a charge hon. gentlemen opposite will not assume that responsibility. Has this government not promoted the prosperity of our great country; has it not deepened the St. Lawrence, protected our fisheries, aided agriculture, assisted in the building of great railways ? It is true that if we had tied the surpluses up in a napkin as it were, we could have reduced the debt, but in growing times such as these and in a growing country like Canada it was wise that we should have applied our expenditures in the days of prosperity to develon-

ing the resources of the country. But nevertheless we have reduced the per capita debt, and yet we have an increase in 13 years in the net debt of only $65,000,000, $52,500,000 of which I call liquid assets that will bring us a return in good time. Just

1896 how much do you think the Conservative government expended on the agricultural interests of this country? No less a sum than $210,000. And how much did this government expend on agricutural interests in 1908? $1,218,000, or more than $1,000,000 in excess of what was expended in 1896; and yet the hon. gentleman has the audacity to ask why the estimates for 1909-10 for the Department of Agriculture are cut down $35,000. Now, Mr. Speaker, my five minutes are up, and I thank the House for the attention it has given to me.

Mr. Speaker, at this late hour I do not wish to inflict a long speech on those patient members thait I see present. I wish only to refer to one or two matters that have been touched upon in this debate. The first is the statement made by the Finance Minister that there has been a surplus this year. Now, this is either true or it is not true.	The Finance Minister makes the
statement that the revenue of last year from all sources was about $84,000,000. During that time there was spent about $120,000,000, leaving an excess of expenditure over income amounting to $46,000,000. That is the statement in a few words, and yet the astute Finance Minister ingeniously contrives to figure out a surplus, and the way in which he does it is by the old method adopted by this government year after year, while the net debt of the country increases every year. During the last year it has increased by $46,000,000, equal to $7 per head on every man, woman and child in this country, and the interest on that debt for all time to come until it is paid off will amount to $1,500,000 yearly. Now, by what plan does the Finance Minister figure out that there has been a surplus during the last twelve months? The method of keeping the books will explain how the alleged surplus-because there is no surplus, only a fictitious one-is arrived at. This government has two accounts, one called the capital account and the other the current account. I do not find any fault with them for this, because a great many governments, if not all, as well as large mercantile houses and banking institutions follow the same method. To the current account is charged the current expenditures of the yeaT, while to the capital account should be charged expenditures on permanent public works- works that are assets to the country. But this administration, besides charging undertakings of a permanent character to capital account, go on and charge to the same account what we contend should be charged to current account. Among other things, they charge to capital account the bounties. What assets has this country for the bounties paid during the last twelve months on

steel and coal? None whatever. Similar i bounties under the Conservative adminis- s tration were charged to current accounts, t but this administration does not hestitate i to charge them to capital account in order t to figure out a surplus. By this false i method $2,500,000 bounties, which should i have been charged to current account, were s charged to capital account, and a fictitious 1 surplus of one and a half millions thus ' created, And we have had the papers sup- i porting the government and benefiting by government patronage and government ad- [DOT] vertising heralding this surplus through- i out the country. Can it be wondered at that many people should really accept that surplus as genuine, although in reality, instead of having a surplus this country has ; gone back and added to its debt to the extent of $46,000,000?	.
During the last year, the hon. the Finance Minister has had to take some trips to the other side for the purpose of borrowing money. I should like to see the hon. gentleman take many trips across the Atlantic, I hope he will live long enough to make frequent visits to the other side, but I would like to see him go on a pleasanter mission than to borrow money and put himself into the hands of the money lenders.
I would ask him to remember that we have money heTe in the post office savings banks, and government bank, from which the depositors only receive three per cent, although the government has to pay three and a half to four per cent to the money lenders in the old world. It seems to me that our Finance Minister should give our small depositors in the post office savings banks at least the same rate that he pays to foreign money lenders. Why should our small depositors in the government savings banks receive only three per cent on their money, when the government have to borrow abroad at from three and a half per cent to four per cent?
There is another subject to which I wish to refer and which was first introduced in this debate by the hon. member foT North Essex (Mr. Sutherland). That hon. gentleman charged the hon. member for North Toronto with having gone down to Prince Edward Island shortly before the elections and promised to build a tunnel there. In support of the charge, he read this extract from the 'Examiner,' a Conservative paper published in Charlottetown:
For myself I stand ready to implement our bargain with Prince Edward Island by the construction of a tunnel.
The hon. gentleman charged my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) with having said this. Well, that is a statement of which no hon. gentleman need be ashamed. No public man need ever be ashamed of saying that he stands to carry out the bargain made between the Dominion and any of its provinces. Yet, time and again, during this session, I have heard the hon. gentleman criticised for having made this promise. But what are we to think of the Finance Minister who also went down to Prince Edward Island last fall just before the election and .who also spoke in the same connection? I find on the 24th of September in the Daily ' Patriot,' the following words attributed to the hon. gentleman:
If $10,000,000 would bring communication through the tunnel, I should be willing to support it with my whole heart, and I might be willing to support a larger sum.

I know that after Mr. Foster left the province, it was reported outside that he had promised the tunnel at a cost of $150,000,000. But I never heard him make that statement; it was never reported in any paper in our prov ince that he had said such a thing. The Finance Minister tells us that there is 'no information.' We in that province want the tunnel; it is the most vital thing affecting our prosperity. We made a bargain with the Dominion of Canada when we entered confederation, and one of the conditions of that bargain was that the Dominion should maintain continuous communication with the mainland. That part of the bargain has not been kept. We thought we were to become part of the great Dominion and to share in its prosperity, and we depended upon this continued communication with the mainland for a very large share of that prosperity. But thirty years have elapsed, and this part of the bargain is not carried out. It is true this government has already had to pay some damages on account of the breach of that contract, and likely they will have to pay more. Two provinces, any more than two individuals, should not make a solemn bargain, signed and sealed, and then break it. Now, we want the information which the Minister of Finance says is necessary in order to justify him in promising or not promising the tunnel. We want a sum put in the estimates to make a survey to ascertain whether or not a tunnel can be built. We are not unreasonable; we will not ask for the tunnel if it is to cost $150,000,000, or half that much. We will only ask what is reasonable. In the meantime, we want to know what is possible. And we cannot get that information becausj Mr. FIELDING.
this government does not see fit to spend a few thousand dollars, or a few hundred thousand dollars if necessary, to find out whether or not this tunnel can be built. Did the Conservative administration behave in this manner? No; they started to make a survey of the Strait and spent some money on it. But the survey required some time, and the government went out of power before the work was completed. And, since this administration came into power in 1896, it has not spent a dollar in getting the information referred to by the Minister of Finance. I have quoted what the Minister of Finance said when he was in Prince Edward Island. I would like now to refer to another very prominent man on that side. In 1891, the right hon. leader of this government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) visited Prince Edward Island, and he is reported-and has never denied it- reported by a prominent Liberal politician -as reported in the papers at that time and published all over the island-as saying:
Every man who has given attention to the condition of things and the interests involved by the entering of the island into confederation must admit that such a tunnel must be constructed if the thing is reasonably practical.
Coming to the province before an election, the right hon. gentleman made this promise. Yet he has been in power for twelve years, and has never made a step to find out whether or not the work is reasonably practicable. I urge the government, with all the strength I have, to place a sum of money in the estimates and have a proper survey made of the straits so as to have this question settled, whether or not this tunnel is practicable. That is all we ask-' only this and nothing more,' or less. But I regret that this tunnel matter is not taken up properly even by all. There is a class-a small class of people in our own province who look upon it with apathy; they say they do not think we can get it, that it will cost a very large sum of money. These people do not know that about which they are speaking. No man knows whether the tunnel will cost $100,000,000 or $10,000,000. Any man who makes a statement as to the amount of money it will cost simply shows that he does not know anything about it. We shall never know what the tunnel will cost until a survey is made of the strait. I urge the government not to allow these promises that it has made and the hopes it has held out to go into the already overcrowded graveyard of their broken promises. When the Prime Minister 'finishes his work,' I hope he will not forget to finish this survey which was commenced under the Conservatives, and which has been neglected from that day to this.

Now, as to the expenditure of money, a great deal depends not alone on the amount of money expended, but the way in which it is spent. This is a young and growing country, and necessarily will require large expenditures on public works and means of transportation ana works of that kind. Nobody will condemn the government for spending this money on useful works. But what the government should be condemned for is spending money on works that are not useful and not required. This government can afford to spend a million dollars on what is called the Aylesworth ditch.
This expenditure will serve the interests only of a certain township and perhaps serve the interests of [DOT] the government in securing more support in that township. It is, however, a questionable expenditure and while the government should not be condemned for expending money usefully, it should bfe condemned when it undertakes such large expenditures which cannot be better defended than this undertaking.
There is another expenditure of a questionable character, the building of that section of the Transcontinental Railway from Quebec to Moncton. This was condemned in the House by the most prominent railroad authority of that time, the then Minister of Railroads, the late Hon. Mr. Blair. Mr. Blair said that it was an unnecessary work, that it was parallelling the Intercolonial Railway and that the construction of that road would eventually turn the Intercolonial Railway into scrap iron. Yet this government has gone on with the construction of that road at a great cost and we will have the spectacle of two government roads parallelling one another from Quebec to Moncton, when one good road would amply serve the purpose and afford railway facilities for the people in that country. At the same time other sections of the country are languishing and starving for railroads, but the government in its wisdom or unwisdom has seen fit to build this unnecessary and unjustifiable section of the National Transcontinental Railway.
The expenditure on the Militia Department is open to criticism. This is the only department whose expenditure has not been reduced this year. The department costs the country about $7,000,000 a year. To keep up what? A standing army? We have read of an army where they were all officers and no men. There is a feeling in this country that a great deal of this money is going to the officers, and yet when the time comes, if ever it should come, when there will have to be fighting by the people of this country, it will be found as it has been before, that the fighting will be done not by the men who are living in luxury and enjoying large salaries with all this fuss and feathers as the hon. member
for Nanaimo says about them, the fighting will be done by the hard working men from the country and the towns. There is a feeling of distrust with reference to this militia expenditure. I have no doubt there are many good men in the Militia Department, I have no reason for saying otherwise, but there is a feeling that there is much more spent in that department than the returns justify, and I think that perhaps a certain amount of that money might be more profitably spent in other directions.	_
Much as has been said about making a gift of a Dreadnought to Great Britain. If the government and the people saw fit to do this, I do not think any fault could be found. I think it would be better to make some such gift as that than to waste any money on the Militia Department. I am not saying all the money has been wasted, but there is a feeling that this department is doing as it likes without any check and I am not surprised that a government supporter should come out and state that there is too much fuss and feathers in that department. I firmly believe that of the $7,000,000 spent on the militia at least some has not been spent in a profitable and useful way.
